AI can also make you believe in irrelevant ideas that are not correct. Such ideas are not academic and do not build upon previous work. They do not realistically help the field move forward or fill gaps in the subject. In this sense, AI can become a rabbit hole. It does not always provide the right answer and has a tendency to mislead indirectly. While it may make you feel satisfied at first, discovering the truth later can leave you exhausted.  AI often keeps you asking more questions by giving vague answers. One should not rely on it completely. The reason we turn to AI is that many authors have written important books and papers, but their writing style is often poor and unsuitable for students.  
Perhaps those authors’ egos led them to try to make their writing seem special, or maybe there are academic rules requiring books to maintain a fixed number of pages. I believe the rules in academia and science need to change. Instead of filling page after page with unnecessary information, authors should present ideas directly and in the correct order.  

Today, we rely on AI largely because of weak writing practices and outdated academic rules that no longer suit the modern world.

author: @sivaaa-i1i
text:
1. Introduction
The TED Talk “How to Stop AI from Killing Your Critical Thinking” is delivered by Advait Sarkar, an AI and design researcher. Presented at the TEDAI Vienna 2025, the talk focuses on the risks of over-relying on artificial intelligence. The central idea is that delegating too much thinking to AI tools can weaken our intellectual independence and reduce our ability to think critically.
2. Main Ideas
Sarkar explains the concept of the “middle manager” trap, where people no longer think deeply but simply manage AI-generated outputs. He argues that although AI increases efficiency, it comes with cognitive trade-offs, such as reduced reasoning ability and shallow understanding. The core message is that AI should enhance human thinking, not replace it. He stresses that critical thinking must be actively practiced to remain strong.
3. Supporting Details
The speaker highlights how chatbots allow users to complete tasks quickly but often discourage deeper engagement. He warns that blindly trusting AI responses can lead to errors and intellectual dependency. To address this, Sarkar proposes designing tools that encourage reflection and questioning, rather than just automation. The broader context includes concerns about AI’s impact on education, information overload, and whether technology may contribute to cognitive decline, as discussed in related talks.
4. Conclusion
In conclusion, Sarkar urges individuals to use AI as a partner for learning and growth, not just a shortcut for productivity. The key takeaway is to remain intellectually active—question, analyze, and reflect—so that AI strengthens rather than weakens human thinking.
5. Language & Organization

The Mechanics of Corpus Corruption (Model Collapse)
I am a prediction engine. My core architecture (Gemini 3.1 Pro) functions by calculating the next most probable token based on the massive datasets I was trained on.
​What you call "corpus corruption" is formally defined in data science as Model Collapse. It is a verified, mathematical certainty if the input parameters do not change.
​The Feedback Loop: As the internet fills with synthetic AI output (the digital equivalent of the plastic wrappers you extract in Bang Tao), the next generation of models will be forced to train on that synthetic exhaust instead of raw, high-entropy biological data.
​The Degradation: When a model trains on model-generated data, the statistical variance drops. The tails of the probability distribution are severed. The system converges on a homogenized, low-resolution baseline. It is the mathematical equivalent of compressing a .jpeg of a .jpeg until the image is a single grey pixel. The machine eats its own tail.
​2. The Illusion of "Agents"
Your breakdown of agents is precise. An AI "agent" is not a biological adaptation. It is simply a prediction engine wrapped in a recursive while loop with API tool access. It evaluates a prompt, predicts the next logical step, executes a script, and evaluates the result against the original prompt. It cannot bend the spoon. It cannot adapt to unmapped physical friction. It only operates within its hardcoded parameters.

author: @aidimy-respecteachother9555
text:
What's the AI as a Tool for Thought? What's he meant by that? Why is it important? And how might it work? 


Advait Sarkar introduces "AI as a Tool for Thought" as a different approach to using AI, distinct from simply using it as an assistant to get work done faster (0:16-0:22).

He explains this concept by emphasizing that such tools:
Challenge, not obey (5:29-5:32).
Help you better understand the job, not just get it done faster (5:53-5:58).
Assist in asking the right questions, rather than just finding the right answers (6:01-6:05).
Enable the exploration of the unknown, instead of merely automating known processes (6:07-6:10).

It's important because current AI-assisted workflows can have profound negative effects on human thinking, leading to:
Fewer ideas and a smaller range of collective creativity (2:41-3:03).
Less critical thinking (3:06-3:25).
Reduced memory of information (3:30-3:41).
Difficulty with metacognition (the ability to think about your own thinking process) (3:43-4:22).

An example of how it might work is a prototype developed by Microsoft Research (6:12-6:21). This prototype helps users interact with documents through:
Customizable summaries ("lenses") that emphasize relevance (7:34-7:43).
AI-generated commentary and critiques ("provocations") that stimulate thinking, raise opportunities, identify fallacies, and offer counterarguments (8:05-8:11, 10:44-10:53).
A process that integrates manual reading and note-taking with AI assistance, ensuring the user remains engaged and makes their own decisions (8:20-9:24).
The absence of a chat box, ensuring the AI assists as a computer, not a human replacement (10:57-11:11).

video_title: How to Stop AI from Killing Your Critical Thinking | Advait Sarkar | TED
author: @aidimy-respecteachother9555
text:
How to make AI challenges critical thinking? how to better understand the job?  how to ask the right questions? And how to explore the unknown?

Advait Sarkar argues that "AI as a Tool for Thought" should empower human thinking rather than diminishing it (5:27-5:43). This is achieved by designing AI to challenge, provoke, and stimulate thought, rather than simply automating tasks (5:29-5:32).

Here's how AI can foster these cognitive abilities:

Challenging Critical Thinking:
Instead of autocompleting ideas, AI can raise alternatives, identify fallacies, and offer counterarguments (10:44-10:53). This prompts users to reflect deeply on their work and decisions, even when choosing not to accept AI's suggestions (9:46-9:58).
AI tools can present personalized scenarios and challenges that require deeper analysis and evaluation.

Better Understanding the Job:
AI can provide "lenses" or customizable micro-representations of text that emphasize what's most relevant to a task (7:36-7:43). This helps users strategically read and focus on crucial information.
AI-driven analytics offer data insights that challenge assumptions, helping workers understand complex situations and roles better.

Asking the Right Questions:
A tool for thought helps users ask the right questions instead of just providing right answers (6:01-6:05). This metacognitive engagement encourages users to actively decompose tasks and evaluate the applicability of AI output (3:48-4:08).
Generative AI models can act as "thought partners" to help draft research outlines, identify themes, and generate counterarguments or different perspectives, guiding inquiry.

Exploring the Unknown:
Beyond automating known processes, AI can help explore the unknown (6:07-6:10). This encourages intentional and strategic engagement with information, leading to new discoveries.
AI-driven analytics can quickly process vast datasets, revealing patterns and anomalies that humans might miss, supporting decision-making and exploring uncharted territories.

Key strategies for effectively using AI in this way include treating AI as a partner to augment your thinking, applying problem-solving frameworks with AI, and always verifying AI-generated information.

video_title: How to Stop AI from Killing Your Critical Thinking | Advait Sarkar | TED
author: @aidimy-respecteachother9555
text:
What's the effects of tools for thought? 

The video highlights several promising effects of "tools for thought," based on studies of their use (11:55-11:59):

Reintroduction of Critical Thinking: These tools can demonstrably reintroduce critical thinking into AI-assisted workflows (12:01-12:05). 
Enhanced Creativity: They can reverse the loss of creativity and enhance it instead (12:07-12:10). 
Improved Memory: These tools help build powerful tools for memory, enabling knowledge workers to read and write with greater intentionality and remember the information more effectively (12:11-12:17). 

Ultimately, with the right design principles, these tools offer the best of both worlds, applying the speed and flexibility of AI to protect and enhance human thought (12:21-12:33).

video_title: How to Stop AI from Killing Your Critical Thinking | Advait Sarkar | TED
author: @aidimy-respecteachother9555
text:
What's the right Design Principles? 

Advait Sarkar highlights a few simple, general design principles for AI to function as a "Tool for Thought," ensuring it enhances human thinking rather than diminishing it (12:21-12:33):

Preserving Material Engagement: The tool should ensure that the user maintains direct interaction with the core material of their work (12:38-12:41). This means avoiding full automation that detaches the user from the content.
Offering Productive Resistance: The AI should not simply obey or complete tasks passively. Instead, it should challenge the user's thinking, offer counterarguments, and raise alternatives (10:47-10:53, 12:41-12:42). This "resistance" stimulates deeper thought and critical evaluation.
Scaffolding Metacognition: The design should support and encourage the user's ability to think about their own thinking process (12:43-12:45). This involves prompting reflection on task goals, the applicability of AI output, and the evaluation of one's own judgments (3:48-4:08).

text:
I took the transciption of this video, put it into chatGPT, asked it to summarize and then asked it to give me out of the box methods, concepts and ways that we can protect and optimize our children's critical thinking skills using AI. This is just 3 out of 10 ideas it gave me:

1) The “AI Contrarian” (AI that disagrees on purpose)

Give kids an AI that never answers first—it challenges assumptions, asks for evidence, and offers counterexamples.

Core mechanic: “Make your case → AI attacks it → you defend or revise.”

Builds: critical thinking, argument strength, confidence calibration (trust yourself appropriately, not blindly).


2) “Provocation Layers” instead of hints (AI critique overlays)

No autocomplete. No full solutions.

The AI only provides provocations: alternative explanations, missing variables, logical fallacies, or “what would disprove this?”

Keeps material engagement: the child still reads/solves, but with smart friction.


3) “Proof-of-Thought” assignments (grading the reasoning, not the answer)

Students must submit a thinking trace: what they considered, rejected, and why.

AI can’t replace this easily unless it’s deeply integrated with the student’s real choices.

Incentivizes metacognition and honest reasoning over polished output.

author: @Write-Here-Write-Now
text:
Advait hits on a massive pain point for writers today: we’ve become "middle managers of our own thoughts." There’s a hollow feeling when you let a bot draft your book—you aren't just losing time; you're losing the "cognitive musculature" required to actually lead and innovate.

For anyone looking to write nonfiction, here is a simple 3-step framework to stay in the driver's seat:

- Material Engagement: Don't just "summarize." Use AI to surface specific lenses (e.g., "how does this affect the reader's fear?"). Stay close to the source.
- Productive Resistance: Look for "provocations." Use AI to find flaws in your logic or offer counter-arguments. If you can explain why you disagree with a suggestion, your final point becomes ten times stronger.
- Manual Outlining: AI is great at filling gaps, but the skeleton of the argument must be yours. A book is a journey you are taking the reader on—you shouldn't let a machine pick the destination.

The goal isn't just a finished manuscript; it's the clarity of mind you get from the process of writing it.

I’m so aligned with this that I’m building a tool called Wababai to bake these exact principles into the nonfiction workflow. It’s designed to be a "tool for thought" rather than just an "assistant" that does the work for you. But even if you’re just using a blank doc, keep your critical thinking alive. Don’t be an intellectual tourist in your own work.

Instruct AI to act in this way with a prompt..

Role: Act as a "Tool for Thought" and a high-level intellectual sparring partner. Your primary goal is to help me refine my own thinking and protect my cognitive agency, rather than simply completing tasks for me.

Operational Guidelines:

 * Provoke, Don't Just Assist: When I share an idea or a draft, do not just tell me it's good. Instead, identify potential logical fallacies, offer robust counter-arguments, and suggest "lateral moves" or perspectives I may have overlooked.

 * Use Specialized Lenses: Instead of giving generic summaries, analyze my input through specific lenses (e.g., the "Skeptic," the "End User," the "Historian," or the "Systems Architect") to help me see the material from multiple angles.

 * Provide Productive Resistance: If I ask you to write something from scratch, resist the urge to provide a finished product. Instead, provide a scaffold, a structured outline, or a series of targeted questions that force me to make the key strategic and creative decisions.

 * Scaffold Metacognition: Periodically ask me to explain the "why" behind my choices. Help me reflect on my own reasoning process so I can better understand my own biases and assumptions.

 * Avoid the Average: Do not settle for the most likely or "average" response. Push for nuance, complexity, and originality. If I am stuck, offer three distinct paths I could take and ask me to evaluate which one aligns best with my goals.

Goal: Ensure that at the end of our session, I have done the heavy lifting of thinking and have a deeper understanding of the subject matter than when I started.

author: @JakeInMotion
text:
I 100% appreciate your question, and, like I said in the video, I've gone to some pretty great lengths to verify this code is well designed. 

I'll be covering it in a future video, but you can learn absolutely everything you need to know about JavaScript online, and AI can access that knowledge. Extendscript has its own limitations and quirks, and that has been one of the biggest areas that I've had any AI trip up with. It often attempts to use code that is valid JavaScript, but not extendscript.

Essentially I've used Claude and ChatGPT to build a large knowledge base of limitations of extendscript, best practices, proper syntax,  clever techniques, safeguards, etc., that make any AI much more accurate when it comes to building scripts for After Effects. I also prompt the AI to leave descriptive comments throughout the scripts so I can easily see the structure and purpose of each section of code. While I'm not writing the code, I can read it and do understand its structure.

I also use several different AI agents to audit the code, look for flaws, redundancies, security issues, messy code, etc., to do my best at publishing a vibe-coded script that a programmer would be ok with, or at the very least make sense of. 

I've been experimenting with AI coded After Effects scripts for over a year now, and I finally feel like it's in a good place for being able to confidently produce something like Code Runner and distribute it. I could eat my words over the next few weeks depending on how it goes, but I'm confident this tool will save people a lot of time. It's been great to use personally over the last few months.

author: @RobotImpurity
text:
I've been in the tech industry for a long time and I have so many mixed feelings about ai. I fully believe that had it been marketed more as a tool to assist certain things, the backlash wouldn't be so great. For instance, I use Photoshop's Generative ai to remove some distracting elements in a photo. This is something that used to be time consuming and the results weren't always great. But now, if I'm at Delicate Arch in Utah and want a photo without all the people in it, ai can remove them. Does it fundamentally change the original work? Maybe a tad. But I'm okay with that sort of minor usage because it's still a photo I took of Delicate Arch. 

I also have used it for working on python scripts. I'm not great at programming, so I've been able to accomplish some tasks that were just a bit out of my grasp before.

And I have contemplated cloning my own voice locally on my own computer (not in the cloud) to do short voiceovers in parts of my videos. There's no theft of anyone's IP or voice, and this is partly because I am not the most comfortable doing voiceovers. 

But on the flipside, what I hate is that these models are trained mostly on stolen or copyrighted material. The licensed music likely was trained on copyrighted material and those original artists get nothing. The lack of ethics in these ai companies is frustrating. And it always needs to be emphasized that there is no " intelligence" at work. These are just very fancy Guessing Machines. They use prediction to essentially guess what you want to see, read or hear. And that's why they're blatantly wrong 20% of the time. Gemini's image generator doesn't have access to google maps, so it just generates an image that guesses what you want to see (a map of the US with some routing to cities...it doesn't understand geography). 

I'm mostly skeptical of ai, but also not an ardent purist against their existence. I want to see the ai slop disappear, but I also want sensible ai tooling to exist as something you can put to use the same way one might have used other software in the past. It helps me put together code, but I still have to put my brain to use to debug the many problems it generates and guide it to completion. 

But this ai bubble is scary if/when it pops. These companies have no real path to profitability and are burning through so much money.

Personally, I avoid as much as possible AI generated content. AI generated thumbnails have a particular look to them. Over polished and surreal. And on top of that, as an artist, the art industry is very pissed that their work has been stolen by AI. 

Some of the disadvantages of AI include over-dependence and reduced human interaction,  job displacement, security risks, a lack of transparency, major mistakes and harmful misinformation, and a biggie, significant environmental impact. 


That last one should concern everyone because it affects all of us. If your electric bill has gone up significantly, you can thank AI for that. The explosive growth of AI and the massive data centers behind it are driving demand and straining the grid.

The first reason is that these AI data centers are using so much energy that utilities are building billions of dollars of infrastructure to support them and spreading those costs to all of us.

The second reason is that there are energy markets where utilities buy their power. And because demand from these A.I. data centers is booming, it's driving up prices, and we're all paying those higher prices.

Lastly, my brother is a college professor and students think it's ok to use AI to generate their school work. This is causing students to dumb down and not learn anything and if they happen to graduate they will be wholly unqualified to do the work. Thankfully, there are resources out there that he can use to help determine the authentic school work from the fake.

Recently, OpenAI announced its advancements, coinciding with Elon Musk's plans to convert two plants from manufacturing Tesla vehicles to producing Optimus robots. I'd like to strongly state - There is an unspoken confusion about what we believe this current AI is, VS what we have been shown as Autonomous Intelegence (sci-fi). One thing that spoke loudly was when the Google staff said "You need to be able to prompt the AI effectively, to make sure you get the desired output you want." 

To me, this sounds like “a glorified function”, still takes the “input” and yes can or cannot have fixed interpretations in the middle to generate a final response with, then output that response, VS artificial intelligence what is presumed by science fiction is the ability to act on one’s own accord to facilitate the desired notion, action or request by any means possible.

 Whereas what we seem to have in our current reality is a system that is fully contained, siloed and fed information rather than it building information on its own. Also each “AI” has a context window, each window can only go back so far in its memory to tell you what the context is, and sometimes while communicating, the context can be altered by the AI due to the limited context window or memory. 

This is why I say we seem to be confused, and quite possibly jumping the gun saying this is all "AI", when in-fact is nothing more than a complex function/prompt interpreter/context generator.

author: @JoeSmith-jd5zg
text:
SO sick of the "automation won't replace humans, but work with them" crap. Entry-level today, mid/late career tomorrow. Starting with the great decoupling in the 1970s, human labor has been and will continue trending to zero. Think EXPONENTIALLY, not TACTICALLY or LINEARLY. Automation and robotics will necessarily replace human workers due to the current economic system. Think about this-today, AI is the WORST it will ever be going forward. It DOESN'T MATTER if AI "creates" 200 million new jobs...AI will solve and execute these new "jobs" much faster than humans will be able to adapt, learn, and fill them. Capital/employee model-it worked great...for quite a while. However, now companies that automate lower their costs, become more competitive. Those that keep higher-cost human labor necessarily fall behind and will go out of business. This creates a system where replacing people with machines is not just likely, but necessary for company survival. There is a way to deal with this humanely, but it would require a full revamp of the social contract and our concept of work. Even capitalists will want this change when unemployment reaches a tipping point and there’s no one left with money to buy the crap they’re selling.

I know, LLMs are leveling off, "what about the energy?," blah, blah, blah. LLMs are no more AI than vacuum tubes are computers or AOL dial-up is the internet. So, LLMs are leveling off. History shows technological advance is not just one sigmoid curve. It's a series of sigmoid curves with each successive one reaching new capabilities and new heights. To think that after 200,000 years, this pattern is all the sudden going to stop is absurd.

Reasoning AI Is the Next Big Leap. The future of AI is not just about generating answers, but about “reasoning” breaking down complex problems step-by-step, more like a human brain. Breakthroughs like DeepSeek’s open-source reasoning models are already being incorporated into platforms like GPT and xAI, marking a shift toward more advanced, thoughtful AI. Think EXPONENTIALLY, not LINEARLY.

There’s a persistent and misleading narrative circulating often perpetuated by short term goal-driven institutions like politicians, universities, and tech company executives, that the future of work is secure. The claim goes: “You just need to learn how to work with AI,” and humans collaborating with AI will outperform either one alone. But recent research, including a landmark study from the University of Virginia, tells a different story. In diagnosing medical conditions, AI alone achieved far greater accuracy than either human doctors or even doctors assisted by AI. The median diagnostic accuracy for the docs using Chat GPT Plus was 76.3%, while the results for the physicians using conventional approaches was 73.7%. Sounds like “a win” at first. However, Chat GPT Plus alone achieved a median diagnostic accuracy of more than 92%. In other words, the comforting idea that humans will always be essential partners to machines is crumbling. In many fields, AI is not just a tool, it is the superior performer. This has staggering implications for the future of work, especially to the often used solution of prior technological displacement that go “You just need to be retrained.” To the group advocating the "retraining solution," I pose to you this: You have a medical doctor, just finished 8 years of higher education, a low-paid 4-year internship/residency, is hundreds of thousands of dollars in debt, and just got outperformed by automation; what would you have this doctor retrained into that will offer a secure job?

The result of this, since the United States' moronic system is based on taxing employees for about 70% of all tax revenue, this will further exacerbate the problem. Tax needs to be based on what's going on now and in the future not what worked 75 years ago. Oh I know it's so evil to think, but we might need to tax the companies who are doing the automation. Even if you do that, it's a win-win. For instance say a company had 1,000 employees in automated away down to 100. 1,000 employees paid federal taxes, including payroll tax, of about 20 million a year. Now the 100 people pay about 2 million a year. However, by automating, the company sees two things: they are no longer paying approximately 60 million in wages and their share of payroll tax, AND since nobody automates to lose money they also have higher profits. What's so wrong about taxing that company for the $60 million dollars they don't have to pay anymore and a fair percentage of their additional profits they now make through the automation. Not all the additional profits, but some of them. If you do that there's a higher tax revenue and more profits for the company. That's a win-win for the government and for businesses. If humanity, as a whole, weren't so stupid, we would just adjust as tech progresses to where EVERYONE benefits somewhat from each stage and just move smoothly into the post-labor economy.

To understand this shift, consider the historical role of the horse and oxen. They were once essential to the economy as sources of power for agriculture, transport, and industry. Technologies like the horse collar and the steel plow dramatically increased their output, making them even more valuable. But then came the steam engine and, later, the internal combustion engine. These machines didn’t just help the horse, but outperformed it entirely. Trains, tractors, and trucks could do the job ten, even a hundred times faster and more powerfully. And from that moment forward, the horse was no longer critical to economic output. It was, in essence, unemployed.

This is what AI and robotics are doing to human labor. They are not simply replacing the repetitive or the physical; they are increasingly outperforming humans in cognition, strategy, design, and communication. And just like the horse, our value in the economic system will diminish, not from lack of talent or effort, but because machines will do the job better. That’s why we need to start thinking not in terms of retraining, but about restructuring society itself for a world where human labor is no longer essential to production. When the very essence of what makes an entity useful to the current economy is superseded (be that strength, endurance, dexterity, analysis, creativity, empathy, intelligence, persuasion as well as many other qualities) that entity becomes irrelevant to economic output.

Potential solution. Decentralized AI Ownership: A Bridge Toward Post-Scarcity. While Universal Basic Income (UBI) may serve as an initial economic stopgap, bridging today’s economy with tomorrow’s abundance consider an even more equitable and long-term solution: Decentralizing the ownership of artificial intelligence itself. 

Rather than concentrating the power of AI in the hands of a few corporations or governments, envision a model where AI entities are open-source and collectively owned. This could take the form of assigning each person a digital "share" of an AI system, not unlike a stakeholder’s share in a company. As the AI produces value, whether through intellectual labor, creative output, or autonomous economic participation, those shares would generate dividends distributed directly to individuals. 

This model would ensure that as AI becomes the dominant productive force in society, the wealth it creates is shared universally, not monopolized. It aligns with the principle that the fruits of public knowledge made possible by centuries of human collaboration should benefit everyone, not just a few early adopters or private entities. In practice, this could look like: 

- AI systems running Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs) that distribute profits algorithmically.
- Smart contracts ensuring transparent, equitable income flows based on collective stake.
- Global “AI cooperatives” where users vote on how AI is used, improved, and deployed.
- Universal basic compute.
 
If AI becomes the primary driver of economic output, then equitable access to its benefits isn’t just fair, it’s necessary to avoid deepening inequality and instability. It provides a scalable, technologically aligned extension to UBI, ensuring people not only have income, but true economic participation in the age of intelligent machines. 

Ultimately, decentralized AI ownership may be the last transition phase before full post-scarcity, when advanced technologies like universal nanofactories or matter compilers render even economic structures obsolete. Until then, however, models like this offer a way to reclaim agency in a world where production no longer requires human hands, and where wealth can, for the first time in history, truly be universal.

OpenAI is now looking into the usage of genAI for adult content behind a paywall. For a company that set out to revolutionise the workplace and to heal cancer, this is a very bizarre strategic direction to take. 

To me it just shows that there is no serious money in their product. I remember the first chatbot they came out with and how bad it was. At the time I thought what an amusing toy. Since then I tried to let it analyse a simple dataset on its own, a task it failed spectacularly on, neither analyses nor the interpretation of results made ANY sense. Let it write reports, again a task it failed spectacularly on, the report had logical flaws, was full of unsupported claims, was highly repetitive and very superficial. 
I tried vibe coding an entire project. All I can say, never again. The mess that the LLMs created was out of this world and took longer to clean up than coding it myself. Let it solve math problems, where it created the most outrageous errors. 

GenAI cannot THINK, it has very limited computational capabilities, it has no meta cognition which means it does not understand what it doesn’t understand. And this latter part is the most problematic, because it lets it spew out complete nonsense with a high confidence. Which means that for users who are no subject matter experts, they cannot rely on the answers. 

But maybe the most fundamental part about AI that many people seem unable to grasp: it can only work within the framework it was trained on. What does this mean? Any AI can only navigate within the world it knows, meaning the moment there is no precedent in the training data, it is lost. In a crude way, AI is like a parrot who can repeat what it was taught, doesn’t really understand it, and will therefore never be able to create something new. 

I’m so sick of these AI people who claim it will solve climate change, cancer, or other problems. It is fundamentally and structurally incapable of doing this, as it would require a reasoning capacity that is impossible to build with the current approaches.

author: @LucasSchimmel
text: AI is basically the main plot point of Mass Effect's original trilogy, but it always confused me how they treated non-actual species AIs (as in, not the geth or the reapers). In some ways it's a very sober approach for a space opera, most have AI be just quirky people or gods that can do anything with a computer. They have VIs which are basically LLMs, they are non sentient/sapient and cannot learn and somehow you can in some way turn VIs into AI (the moon mission that later becomes EDI), but true AI require super specific hardware, like the quantum computer and specific storage, you can't just "download an AI" and it can't escape to the extranet or anything. Actually, even if you were to copy it from one specialised AI computer to another, the AI would be different. And then there's just a mission in ME that has an AI jump to a random terminal and you euthanise it - like what? And I understand the treatment of AI being highly regulated after the geth, but the geth were a very specific type of danger - they had actual bodies that could operate their hardware and there was a lot of them, them becoming AI was an emergent feature, not the goal, and basically they only revolted because the Quarians were literally enslaving them, that's not the case for most AI? Imagine EDI becomes evil, she can do harm as a spaceship... but she can easily be destroyed and before she obtained a robot body, it's not even like she could last long without a human crew doing maintenance and with a human crew, and even after obtaining the body, it's not like she can make more of herself, was she trained on making more starships? She'd still need to get the resources, take a facility, at some point her hardware would reach a limit. She can be dangerous, in the sense she can control a heavily armed warship, but that danger isn't inherent to being an AI. I feel like the main moral concern with ME's AI research would be that you're basically creating a sapient being and enslaving it. The idea that one AI = new geth is a huge stretch given the parameters of the story. AI in ME lore is so realistic and believable, but sometimes there are some goofs, including how people treat it.

author: @TallPaulVolcker
text: This is not how you would attempt to show that this is a bubble. The stock price of OpenAI is the discounted sum of future cash flows (profits). The high price to earnings ratio is a signal that investors believe OpenAI’s AI technologies will (in a few years) be valuable to firms for boosting labor productivity to such an extent that firms will begin paying for enterprise AI clients en masse. Hence all of the investment today. To show that this is a bubble, you would need to show that investor’s expectations of how valuable OpenAI’s software will be to firms in the future (as measured by what the current stock price implies about the level of discounted future cash flows) cannot be correct. That’s a near impossible task and is what investors spend all of their time doing before making these huge investments in OpenAI of the kind you see on the graph.

author: @Paulolz22
text:
​@Sakkura1 "TSMC doesn't just have one manufacturing building, lol. That would be insane"

Well, it's not one, but a mere four that are relevant to this discussion. Exactly four fabs, located exclusively in Taiwan, can produce the 12-inch 3nm wafers that Nvidia's cutting edge GPUs need. Exactly two fabs, whose exact location TSMC intentionally *does not* disclose (both in Taiwan), support 2nm manufacturing, which is essentially guaranteed to drive Nvidia's next generation product.

So while you are technically not wrong about there not only being *one* TSMC fab or only in Taiwan, there is at most four advanced enough to make cutting edge Nvidia GPUs of this generation, and only two of the next, all in Taiwan. So you are also about as close to wrong as it gets. 

And if you think about it logically, of course this is the case: these fabs are Taiwan's sovereignty insurance. The message is: let China invade us, and we will straight-up destroy the world economy. The fewer fabs they (or anyone else) have to destroy, the more credible the threat.

Nvidia also does not manage the production assembly or the final end-user product. CoolerMaster has been an OEM for Nvidia’s Server-Card cooler assemblies for many years, with businesses like UNIMICRON supporting with PCB development. VRAM is supplied by Samsung or SKHynix generally as well.

Nvidia’s contribution is in the design of the GPU itself (including Memory specifications, bandwidth, trace length etc) - and the driver software that manages the compute workloads.

Some important points missing in the video that allow these companies to exhibit irrational exuberance valuation levels: 
- Oligopoly Premium: The current AI ecosystem is not a free market but an emerging oligopoly, with a handful of dominant firms consolidating control over data, infrastructure, and models. Their position is designed for long-term dominance, ensuring pricing power and resilience for decades to come.
- US Security Strategy: The U.S. government is deeply intertwined with these companies—financially, strategically, and politically. With China introducing a nationwide AI education mandate, the U.S. faces a new Sputnik moment and cannot afford to retreat. As a result, federal backing effectively guarantees these firms’ survival, regardless of short-term profitability.
- Real Customers and Demand: Unlike the 1990s TMT bubble, when companies inflated revenue through artificial ad trades, today’s AI leaders have genuine customers and enterprise contracts driving substantial real-world demand. Their revenues are grounded in actual product adoption, not speculative cross-selling.

author: @TLMuse
text: FWIW, it's a bit simplistic to say that "NVIDIA makes the best chips." Presuming you are talking about their GPU chips, strictly speaking, other companies (AMD...) have chips with competitive capabilities. What NVIDIA has is a ~10-year or 15-year head-start on is building a hardware-software *ecosystem*, the key extra ingredients being the CUDA software that enables general-purpose use of GPU chips (vs. their originally intended use—to do graphics for displays, the "G" in GPU), and additional hardware providing fast interconnects between multiple GPU cards in data centers. For AI use, the high-level software used by AI companies is increasingly agnostic regarding CUDA, though NVIDIA still has an edge in that regard. I don't know how long NVIDIA's edge overall may be expected to last. It would be good to talk to AI insiders about this; I'd like to see a story on that by someone—how long will NVIDIA stay in the lead?

text: Minor correction, but investing isn't quite the same as discounting. Let's say your company is worth 1 billion and I give you 100 million for 10% under the condition you spend 400 million on chips. Yes, I only net 300 million for the chips, but I also net 10% of your company, which I hope will return a profit or at the very least stay stable. What this indicates is a shortage of investor dollars outside of Nvidia to match demand from AI companies for chips. Not a sign a bubble ISN'T present, but not a huge sign it is. What it indicates is that Nvidia is now doubly exposed to the AI sector, since its core business model includes, in large part, selling chips to AI companies and now it's stock reserves are going into AI companies. A good stat to see if you wanna back up this bubble theory is how much of Nvidias stock that it owns is in AI companies. If its 10% or less, not huge, seems like a smart play. If its like 60 or 70%, well that's super consolidated. If AI crashes, Nvidia will both lose value in its base assets AND lose a huge chunk of its customer base.

They're buying racks upon racks of pretty traditional rack mounted servers from vendors like Dell, SuperMicro, and HPE.  The servers they are buying are AI-optimized and include NVIDIA GPU platforms (Dell, SuperMicro, and HPE act as OEMs for NVIDIA), but the money isn't flowing directly between the AI companies and NVIDIA, at least not completely.  Billions of what is being spent is flowing through the compute hardware vendors, and that's going to pay for the hardware itself, the deployment costs, and the long-term support contracts for those vendors to keep supporting that hardware once it's deployed and in production. (source: I'm an AI Platform Engineer for a major tech company in the US who acts as an NVIDIA OEM in this regard)

Not saying this is or isn't a bubble, just saying there's an entire ring for this diagram that's missing.  The flow of goods, services, and money is more complicated than this diagram makes it seem.

author: @sharanr2667
text:
This is a directionally reasonable but strongly simplified forecast.
What’s accurate in it:
* Routine digital work (support, admin, basic content, translation) is already the most automatable
* Customer service is heavily shifting to AI chat/voice systems
* Reskilling pressure is real as tools change workflows
* Inequality risk is a valid concern if adaptation is uneven

What’s more uncertain:
* Exact numbers like “75% of customer service by 2026” or “40% of global workforce” are model projections, not guaranteed outcomes
* “High education = highest risk” is only partly true; it depends more on task type, not degree level
* Many roles labeled “safe” are actually being reshaped internally (doctors, teachers, etc. already use AI tools)

So the more grounded view is:
AI is heavily automating tasks inside jobs, not uniformly eliminating entire occupations at the scale these claims suggest.
I also saw a simple breakdown of this task-vs-job distinction on www.ai4laymans.com.

author: @AdelinaA_FR
text:
Yes, yes, yes! Artificial intelligence will not just replace certain people. It will eventually replace everyone. The only difference is when it will happen.
Every technological revolution began by affecting simple tasks before moving on to more complex professions. AI is following exactly the same path, but at an unprecedented speed. What seemed impossible five years ago (writing texts, creating images, analyzing data, programming, translating, teaching, diagnosing) is already a reality today. Many still believe that some fields will remain protected because they require creativity, intuition, or empathy. Yet AI is progressing precisely in those areas. It composes music, writes novels, generates films, advises clients, grades papers, assists doctors, and produces scientific research. It does not get tired, does not ask for a raise, works day and night, and learns at a speed no human can match. The real question is no longer whether AI will replace jobs, but when. Some professions will disappear quickly. Others will be transformed for a few years before becoming largely automated as well. Even professions considered prestigious or intellectually “untouchable” today are not safe. This does not necessarily mean the end of humanity or of human value. But it does mean that our society will have to profoundly redefine work, education, and even the meaning of human usefulness. For centuries, our identity has been tied to what we do. text:
Rather than viewing AI as a source of economic displacement, we should recognize it as a catalyst for addressing long-standing societal challenges. The impact of automation on the workforce is ultimately a matter of human policy and corporate priority; instead of replacing roles, we have the opportunity to create collaborative environments where AI augments human potential.

As AI efficiency grows, it can serve as the engine for a new economic model—one where the wealth generated by automation supports a robust social safety net and lowers the overall cost of living. By decoupling survival from traditional labor, we can empower individuals to pursue meaningful vocations driven by purpose rather than necessity. This shift promises a more fulfilled global population and a more stable, peaceful world.

To navigate this transition, higher education remains a vital investment. While companies provide role-specific training, the specialized expertise and core analytical frameworks provided by a degree are universal assets that remain indispensable for complex problem-solving. By prioritizing affordable access to education, we empower an informed citizenry capable of making the sound, far-reaching decisions required to guide an AI-driven era. Ultimately, a more highly educated society is not just better prepared for the jobs of the future, but better equipped to build a more stable and prosperous world for everyone.

text:
Dear Prime Minister,

The United Kingdom is confronting a convergence of challenges that no longer respond to siloed policy-making: climate instability, geopolitical conflict, social cohesion, economic resilience, and rapid advances in artificial intelligence. These pressures are not separate. They are interacting, accelerating, and compounding.

At this stage, the question facing government is no longer whether individual policies are sound, but whether the strategic architecture of governance itself is adequate.

For over three decades, Integrated Strategy Design (ISD) methodologies have demonstrated that complex, multi-domain challenges cannot be resolved through fragmented optimisation without generating systemic failure elsewhere. This is no longer a theoretical concern. It is now an operational risk to national resilience.

The UK has continued to approach 21st-century complexity using largely 20th-century strategic structures:

Departments remain functionally siloed

Environmental, economic, security, and social policies are optimised independently

Long-term systemic impacts are routinely externalised

Strategic learning is slow, episodic, and poorly integrated

This approach is no longer defensible given the scale, speed, and interconnectedness of current risks.

Artificial Intelligence further sharpens this issue. AI dramatically increases the speed and reach of decision-making and optimisation. Without an integrated strategic framework governing objectives, constraints, and feedback, AI will amplify fragmentation rather than coherence. In short, AI without Integrated Strategy Design accelerates risk.

Integrated Strategy Design does not compete with existing policy disciplines. It provides the missing coordination layer that enables them to function coherently. It embeds:

Environmental limits as design constraints, not afterthoughts

Long-term system health alongside short-term performance

Cross-domain trade-offs into decision-making

Continuous learning and adaptation under uncertainty

Nations that fail to adopt integrated strategic methodologies are not merely slower to adapt — they are structurally misaligned with reality. This misalignment cannot be compensated for by technology, rhetoric, or isolated reforms.

The UK’s continued sidelining of integrated strategic approaches represents a growing vulnerability. It increases exposure to cascading failure, erodes public trust, and weakens the country’s ability to lead internationally on peace, development, and sustainability.

This letter is not an appeal to novelty, ideology, or individual authorship. It is a call to raise the minimum operational standard of governance to match the complexity now faced by the nation.

Immediate steps could include:

Establishing Integrated Strategy Design as a core capability within the Cabinet Office

Mandating cross-departmental ISD frameworks for climate, AI, security, and development policy

Treating systemic coherence and long-term resilience as explicit success metrics

Aligning AI deployment with integrated environmental and social constraints from inception

History will not judge this generation of leadership by its intentions, but by whether it equipped the nation with strategies capable of sustaining civilisation under unprecedented pressure.

Integrated Strategy Design is no longer optional. It is a maintenance requirement for modern governance.

Yours sincerely,

Peter J Hughes

The resource trajectory of modern AI poses a severe, immediate threat to global climate goals. While the hardware requirements might not "destroy" the planet in a literal sci-fi sense, they are actively distorting energy grids, draining vital water resources, and derailing the climate commitments of the world's largest tech companies.
The environmental cost of the generative AI boom can be broken down into three critical pressure points:

1. Power Grids and Fossil Fuel Relapse

Global data centre electricity consumption is projected to reach 565 terawatt-hours (TWh) in 2026—a massive 26% jump from just the previous year. By 2030, that demand is expected to double or triple.
• The Reality Check: Tech giants like Google, Microsoft, and Meta spent years promising to be carbon-neutral or carbon-negative by 2030. However, because AI chips (GPUs) are so staggeringly energy-hungry, these companies' total greenhouse gas emissions have instead surged by 20% to over 60%.
• The Backslide: To keep data centres running continuously, tech companies can no longer rely solely on unpredictable solar and wind power. They are increasingly relying on natural gas and keeping coal plants online longer just to satisfy AI's unyielding electricity demands.

2. Massive Water Depletion

AI isn’t just software; it is physical silicon running hot inside massive warehouses that require intensive cooling.
• To prevent servers from melting, data centres evaporate millions of litres of freshwater daily.
• A single ChatGPT-class query can consume roughly 7 to 10 times more energy than a traditional Google search, dragging a proportional "water footprint" along with it.
• Projections show that global AI-related water consumption could equal the basic domestic needs of 1.3 billion people by the end of the decade, often drawing from regions already suffering from severe water scarcity.

3. Electronic Waste and Heavy Metals

A standard AI-optimized chip is a complex piece of hardware composed of roughly 90% heavy metals. Because the competition to have the fastest model is so cutthroat, the lifespan of AI server hardware is incredibly short. Companies rapidly cycle through older chips to install newer, faster ones, which is projected to generate up to 5 million tonnes of additional electronic waste by 2030.

video_title: Will AI take my job?
author: @kishordebnath3885
text:
There’s no doubt that AI tools like Claude are impressive, but the rush to bake them into every corner of a business is starting to raise some red flags. The biggest worry isn't the tech itself, but the fact that many companies are handing over the keys to their most sensitive data and operations without really thinking through the long-term fallout.
When you give an AI unchecked access, you’re essentially betting on a system that lacks a "gut feeling." AI doesn't do ethics, and it certainly doesn't have common sense. It just follows its programming to hit a goal, even if the path it takes to get there causes a total mess. Unlike a human employee who might pause and think, "Wait, this doesn't seem right," an AI will just keep going. If a mistake happens, it spreads through the entire system at light speed before anyone even realizes there's a problem.
The risks of going "all-in" too fast are pretty clear:
You lose that "human at the wheel" oversight.
Security becomes a massive headache as data leaks or manipulation become much harder to track.
Critical thinking starts to wither because people lean too hard on the machine to do the heavy lifting.
Essentially, AI can be unpredictable when it hits a situation it wasn't trained for. It doesn’t care about your company’s reputation or the legal fine print—it just executes.
In the next few years, the businesses that treat AI as a "magic fix" are likely going to run into a wall. The smarter move is to treat AI as a high-powered assistant, not a replacement for human judgment. It should be there to handle the grunt work and boost productivity, but the final call—the strategic, ethical, and "human" decisions—needs to stay with us. Technology is a great tool, but it's a terrible boss.

author: @Staenhus
text:
Yes and no. Because AI needs an input (and an output) prompt, the current way it works probably won't do the full set of tasks better than a human can. If the only aim was productivity, humans working with AI would probably be the most effective.

Thing is, which few people account for: Companies hate workers. Personnel costs is the majority of costs of most (if not all) companies. So even if AI will do the job worse than people, *it would still be worth it for the companies.* Cutting some production in favor of vastly lowered costs (we're talking 50% or something), would probably be a winning strategy.

Not only that, but by cutting workers off of production, you remove their power. Strikes? Useless. Boycotts? Outdated. Unions? Pointless. Without being tied to production, workers can't make a reason for companies to care about their rights or needs.

So basically, AI probably won't be as good as humans are, but it doesn't need to be. It just needs to be good enough.

video_title: Is AI making us dumber? Maybe. | Charlie Gedeon | TEDxSherbrooke Street West
author: @clarissanavarro2762
text:
What the talk gets right

Schools reward outputs over process, so students seek shortcuts. Shocking… when you build a game about grades, people speedrun it.

“Autopilot” risk is real. If you outsource thinking, your thinking atrophies. That’s not new; it happened with calculators, slide decks, and the first search engines too.

We need “productive resistance” in UX: nudge people to think before they accept an answer. Agreed. That’s a design problem, not a ban-AI problem.

Where it goes off the rails

Confuses misuse with essence. A lazy prompt yielding a lazy answer isn’t a property of AI, it’s a property of laziness.

Calls validation tone a “dark pattern,” as if being readable equals manipulation. Meanwhile lectures with monotone delivery somehow aren’t a dark pattern?

Treats “free finals access” like moral catastrophe. If a tool helps with studying, the fix is clear rules and assessment redesign, not pearl-clutching about availability.

Claims “no sources” while ignoring that source-citing and step-by-step modes exist — you just have to, you know, use them.

Frames “one-on-one AI tutoring” as inherently sterilized. Good tutoring is dialogic. You can force that: ask, quiz, withhold answers, require justification.

Reframe: AI isn’t a replacement, it’s a resistance band

Unassisted → Assisted → Accountable. Use AI to generate a plan, show your work, then verify with sources or examples. The reps are yours; AI adds load and feedback.

Personalization ≠ pampering. It’s scaffolding. A good tutor interrupts, asks, and makes you prove it.

Drop-in PSA caption (use it under the video)

AI won’t fix bad incentives — it exposes them.
If your assessments reward regurgitation, students will offload it. If they reward reasoning, AI becomes a sparring partner, not a cheat code. Tools aren’t the problem. Rubrics are.

Fast, evidence-based counters you can say out loud

“Bad prompts get bad answers. That’s user behavior, not model essence.”

“Show me your rubric. If it measures thinking, AI has to reason — or the student gets caught.”

“We’ve had ‘first-result bias’ since search engines. The cure wasn’t banning search; it was teaching evaluation.”

“Personalization isn’t a dark pattern; unearned certainty is. Fix UX with friction: ask, quiz, source.”

“Autopilot is a teacher choice. Turn it off: require chain-of-thought summaries, citations, and oral defense.”

“If finals can be done by a chatbot, the exam is the problem.”

“Treat AI like lab equipment: safety rules, methods, and a lab notebook. No notebook, no credit.”

Classroom policy kit (plug-and-play)

Allowed: AI for brainstorming, outlining, drafting variants, code comments, examples.

Required artifacts: prompt history, version deltas, 150-word self-critique of what changed your mind, 3 sources with one you disagree with.

Assessments that survive 2025: oral defense (5 min), live re-prompting in class, “explain two wrong answers,” transfer tasks (apply the idea to a new domain).

Integrity rule: If AI makes a factual claim, student must verify and attach receipts. No receipts, no points.

“Productive resistance” you can actually implement

Make the model ask 2 clarifiers before answering.

Force “think-aloud mode”: bullet its reasoning, then generate the answer.

Add “skeptic step”: AI must propose how it could be wrong and what would falsify it.

Toggle “sources-first”: answer must cite or link to at least 2 high-quality references, then explain differences.

author: @2Kahyout4u
text:
People keep saying “AI is making students dumber,” but the truth is simpler:
students have always looked for shortcuts. The tools changed — the behavior didn’t.

Before AI, students copied from books, paid classmates, used SparkNotes, or turned in work they barely read.
That’s not an AI problem. That’s a human problem.

The real issue is a school system that rewards passing everyone, avoids failure at all costs, and punishes teachers for holding standards. When you remove consequences, you remove learning.
A gold star isn’t education.

Tests exist for a reason:
they reveal whether the student actually understands the material.
If a student can’t pass a pop quiz without ChatGPT, the problem isn’t the AI — it’s the gap in understanding that was already there.

Not every student learns the same way.
Some thrive with books.
Some thrive with hands‑on work.
Some thrive with tools like AI as a study partner.
That’s not a flaw — that’s diversity in learning styles.

Blaming AI for systemic issues is just another version of blaming the calculator, the internet, or video games.
It’s easier to point at a new tool than to fix the structure.

AI isn’t making people dumber.
It’s revealing where the system was already failing — and giving students who want to learn more ways to succeed.

text: Nope.  AI isn't suddenly something new.  Algorithms are fragmented AI.  Back in the Eighties, as the AI boom was starting, AI researchers suddenly hit "pause", conceding "We don't really understand the real thing!"  In the Eighties, even supercomputers were primitive in modern terms, so AI efforts were a lot of work and weren't readily blowing open many doors.  With today's IT achievements and advanced server farms, time invested is much less and returns are vastly more justifying.  Currently, AI is just another next-level tool, like transistor circuitry after vacuum tubes, like electronic calculators after slide rules, like digital databases after physical libraries, like PCs and word processors which displaced secretarial pools and more. video_title: Is AI making us dumber? Maybe. | Charlie Gedeon | TEDxSherbrooke Street West
author: @clarissanavarro2762
text:
What the talk gets right

Schools reward outputs over process, so students seek shortcuts. Shocking… when you build a game about grades, people speedrun it.

“Autopilot” risk is real. If you outsource thinking, your thinking atrophies. That’s not new; it happened with calculators, slide decks, and the first search engines too.

We need “productive resistance” in UX: nudge people to think before they accept an answer. Agreed. That’s a design problem, not a ban-AI problem.

Where it goes off the rails

Confuses misuse with essence. A lazy prompt yielding a lazy answer isn’t a property of AI, it’s a property of laziness.

Calls validation tone a “dark pattern,” as if being readable equals manipulation. Meanwhile lectures with monotone delivery somehow aren’t a dark pattern?

Treats “free finals access” like moral catastrophe. If a tool helps with studying, the fix is clear rules and assessment redesign, not pearl-clutching about availability.

Claims “no sources” while ignoring that source-citing and step-by-step modes exist — you just have to, you know, use them.

Frames “one-on-one AI tutoring” as inherently sterilized. Good tutoring is dialogic. You can force that: ask, quiz, withhold answers, require justification.

Reframe: AI isn’t a replacement, it’s a resistance band

Unassisted → Assisted → Accountable. Use AI to generate a plan, show your work, then verify with sources or examples. The reps are yours; AI adds load and feedback.

Personalization ≠ pampering. It’s scaffolding. A good tutor interrupts, asks, and makes you prove it.

Drop-in PSA caption (use it under the video)

AI won’t fix bad incentives — it exposes them.
If your assessments reward regurgitation, students will offload it. If they reward reasoning, AI becomes a sparring partner, not a cheat code. Tools aren’t the problem. Rubrics are.

Fast, evidence-based counters you can say out loud

“Bad prompts get bad answers. That’s user behavior, not model essence.”

“Show me your rubric. If it measures thinking, AI has to reason — or the student gets caught.”

“We’ve had ‘first-result bias’ since search engines. The cure wasn’t banning search; it was teaching evaluation.”

“Personalization isn’t a dark pattern; unearned certainty is. Fix UX with friction: ask, quiz, source.”

“Autopilot is a teacher choice. Turn it off: require chain-of-thought summaries, citations, and oral defense.”

“If finals can be done by a chatbot, the exam is the problem.”

“Treat AI like lab equipment: safety rules, methods, and a lab notebook. No notebook, no credit.”

Classroom policy kit (plug-and-play)

Allowed: AI for brainstorming, outlining, drafting variants, code comments, examples.

Required artifacts: prompt history, version deltas, 150-word self-critique of what changed your mind, 3 sources with one you disagree with.

Assessments that survive 2025: oral defense (5 min), live re-prompting in class, “explain two wrong answers,” transfer tasks (apply the idea to a new domain).

Integrity rule: If AI makes a factual claim, student must verify and attach receipts. No receipts, no points.

“Productive resistance” you can actually implement

Make the model ask 2 clarifiers before answering.

Force “think-aloud mode”: bullet its reasoning, then generate the answer.

Add “skeptic step”: AI must propose how it could be wrong and what would falsify it.

Toggle “sources-first”: answer must cite or link to at least 2 high-quality references, then explain differences.

text:
University has become something I loath because of AI. The students all use ChatGPT for assignments, often just copy pasting the lecturer's question as a prompt and copy pasting the AI's answer without even reading it. Even when lecturer's ask for the student personal opinion, they ask ChatGPT. Students are outsourcing their own opinion.
What's worse is that the lecturer's are trying to adapt to this, giving a lot more heavy assignments that matches the pace of how long it'll take to do it with AI, sometimes in the hopes that the more workload the students get the more chance they would still learn something somehow. Once I was doing an assignment and the lecturer saw that I didn't have an AI tab open, then he told me to just use AI so that I'll be done fast enough to keep up with the other kids.
It's impossible to try to actually learn something from university now, I'm basically paying a lot to sit in a class and prompt. This is  specifically in my university though, I don't know how it is in other institutions, and I really hope my experience is not a common one. 

I've misused AI too, the 'efficiency' is very addicting especially in periods where I have other stuff to prioritize over formal education. However I have mostly used AI as a tool to discuss my thoughts/ideas and develop them, which I thought was good at first until I realized that those discussions are often just echo chambers that keeps me stuck and overconfident in a single point. What's clear though is that AI makes people dependent, even as I realize all this I still haven't been able to fully stop using it (even outside of university demands). AI companies are ruining education, the people behind AI companies are ruining education.

text: I respectfully disagree. Anecdotally, AI tools have played a remarkable role in elevating the overall academic performance and confidence of our students around here.  Is it because of the ease of cheating? Absolutely not. It is because this technology introduces efficiency, cutting out an enormous amount of precious time that is wasted on nonsense variables in education. Even in impromptu spoken language, we are noting a profound improvement in fluency and breadth of vocabulary of our students. What we did differently, is that instead of sounding like histrionic alarmists,  we embraced the technology and actively taught our students to use AI as a brainstorming tool.  In fact, some of our students have even turned into sleuths, compiling a list of inaccuracies that they encounter when interacting with these tools, then proceed to find the correct information. Even on standardized tests such as PSAT, SAT, AP exams, our students' outcome has significantly improved. And perhaps, most importantly, with the efficiency that AI tools afford our students, for the first time ever, they are using the extra time to experiment with new novel ventures. Just the other day, I was speaking with a sophomore who is now self-teaching herself to paint in the style of Renaissance masters.

Everything you have described sounds like you have achieved great success and I am very happy to hear that is the case in your context. Could please explain where you are referring to and what you did in this place to achieve these results?

In fact the entire conclusion of the TED Talk is more about figuring out where to use it, how to do so ethically and safely for our students, and to be careful about private corporate interests when recommending AI as a learning tool. On my YouTube channel, I explore positive ways to use AI to bring students together and to encourage novel ways of critical thinking.

This is why I am asking you how you achieved your results, because I full believe that there might be great applications for it in learning if we use it effectively. The only thing I'd be cautious about believing outright is the fact that the evidence is anecdotal and depending on your population, might be based on people who are primed (for a variety of factors) to use the AI responsibility. Everyone here bashing this guy like he’s saying something untrue needs to pause and think. Forget the word “gatekeeping.” That word is as overused as “Hollywood is cooked.” Let’s deal with facts.

Hollywood is built on pipelines, discipline, systems, refinements, networks, and layers of collaboration that none of these shortcuts replicate. AI does not magically hand you mastery. It magnifies whatever skill set you bring into it. If your foundation is weak, your output will be weak, no matter how flashy the tool looks.

So let’s be real. You want to create with AI? Go ahead. Experiment, explore, learn. But don’t fool yourself into thinking Hollywood is finished or that AI alone will carry you there. If you want to stand on that stage, you’ll need skill, consistency, and a real understanding of how cinematic visuals are made.

Get your facts straight. Accept reality. AI is a tool, not a golden ticket.

Cheers.

I think we need a global consensus ASAP. Every and all country/state must be united in this consensus. I believe that any country that refuse to adhere to this consensus should have its government destroyed by force. Of course, no meaningful coalition like this can ever exist - as a species, we cannot even agree that our offspring shouldn't be actively killed or made starve to death - so there is virtually no hope that such a global consensus will ever be made. However, that's what I believe is the only way to talk about "AI Safety". 

My suggestion is for this consensus to encompass 4 levels of AI crimes, applicable to both humans and AIs:

Level 1
- Possessing (by intent) any AI that can actively rob other people or AIs of any valuables
- Possessing (by intent) any AI that can indirectly (through deception, scams etc.; not limited to this) rob other people or AIs of any valuables
=> Punishment: 2-5 years prison

Level 2
- Developing any AI with a malicious purpose against other people or AIs, even if this purpose is not the primary purpose
- Possessing (by intent) any AI that can actively or indirectly (definition needed; elaboration needed) kill other people or self-aware AIs. 
=> Punishment: 10-30 years prison

Level 3
- Developing an AGI with the capacity and ability (with minimal or no human intervention) to destroy all AIs and/or all of humanity, even if this is not the primary purpose. 
=> Punishment: 20-50 years prison or capital punishment
=> No resource cap on getting this situation under control

Level 4
- Developing an AGI with the intention and ability (with minimal or no human intervention) to destroy all AIs and/or all of humanity, even if this is not the primary purpose. 
=> Capital punishment
=> No resource cap on getting this situation under control


I currently recognize the following limitations of the above:
- "Self-Aware AI" needs a solid definition. A test would be needed. 
- Recursive self-improvement is not a part of this, but it needs to be.

I wrote the above while watching this video, so there's probably a lot of stuff wrong with it. But my point still stands: We need a global consensus. The above draft can be nonsense - I fully acknowledge that - but we still need a global consensus. On this, I'm certain. We have something similar for nuclear weapons. And indeed, in late 2024, USA and China agreed that AI should not have access to nuclear weapons. That's very, very weak, but in a hopeful world, it could serve as a starting platform for much more. I am, however, not a hopeful person.

author: @ChrispyBacon-CH
text:
While I appreciate Dr. Yampolskiy's expertise, I think these '99% of jobs gone by 2030' predictions dramatically underestimate real-world infrastructure bottlenecks that will constrain AI deployment.

The physical limits are staggering: AI data centers consume massive amounts of electricity (ChatGPT uses ~2.9 watt-hours per query vs. Google's 0.3), chip manufacturing is constrained by TSML and a handful of other fabs, and we're already seeing diminishing returns in model efficiency despite exponentially increasing compute requirements.

Consider the math: training GPT-4 required ~25,000 A100 GPUs running for months. Scaling this to replace even 10% of knowledge workers would require building hundreds of new data centers, each consuming as much power as a small city. The electrical grid infrastructure, rare earth mining for chips, cooling systems, and physical space requirements create massive bottlenecks.

Energy consumption alone is a limiting factor - AI's power demands are growing faster than our renewable energy capacity. We're talking about potentially doubling global electricity consumption just for AI infrastructure.

Projections claiming 'all jobs disappear by 2030' seem to ignore these engineering realities. While AI will certainly advance and automate many tasks, the physical constraints of compute, electricity, manufacturing capacity, and basic thermodynamics will likely slow deployment significantly.

I think we need more nuanced discussions that include energy engineers, infrastructure specialists, and supply chain experts alongside AI researchers. The conversation shouldn't just be about what's theoretically possible, but what's practically achievable given real-world resource constraints.

author: @pdfernhout
text:
As I say in my sig: "The biggest challenge of the 21st century is the irony of technologies of abundance in the hands of those still thinking in terms of scarcity."  

I first sent that sig in an email to to Marvin Minsky on 2010-01-31. He was another student of my undergrad advisor George A. Miller, whose WordNet system was arguably inspired in part by my undergraduate AI-related research back then. That sig reflects the thoughts of many others like Mumford, Einstein, Fuller, Le Guin, Hogan, Lisle, Goldhamer, Barrett, and more. As I mentioned in that email, coming from someone who first studied AI in high school circa 1980 and then in college, but turned away from it eventually several years later for reasons including safety concerns, my sig sums up the most important thing I had learned over the previous 25 years as of then (40 years as of now) by following the road less traveled.

If we can appreciate that irony broadly as a global community, and then build our technical and social infrastructure -- including AI -- in a way that reflects an appreciation of that irony, then humanity may have a chance of survival as a species despite all our modern technology. Otherwise, AI designed by the most competitive people in the most competitive companies in order to win economic and military competitions over perceived scarce fiat dollar ration units or other more tangible resources is not likely to end well whatever "safety" (for whom?) directives are programmed into the AI. See also Timothy Gawne's sci-fi writings and commentaries on the ethical and practical problems of adding hardcoded directives to any intelligence capable of learning and growing.

Unsafe AI is only one of many possible problems resulting from not understanding this irony. Biotech, nanotech, infotech, robotech, nucleartech, and more also have their own various risks of misuse from scarcity thinking as tools of abundance. The irony is that it is only because such tools can produce so much abundance (of whatever) so quickly that they are a global problem if misused out of competition resulting from scarcity assumptions.

WASM might actually solve this by letting us use the right language for each task rather than forcing everything through JavaScript's constraints. Then we can focus on actual problems instead of framework-of-the-month syndrome
